source_text: Inluxit dies uictoriae illorum, et processerunt de carcere in amphitheatrum, quasi in caelum, hilares et uultu decori; si forte gaudio pauentes non timore. Sequebatur Perpetua placido incessu, ut matrona Christi, ut dei delicata, uigore oculorum deiciens omnium conspectum. Item Felicitas, saluam se peperisse gaudens ut ad bestias pugnaret, a sanguine ad sanguinem, ab obstetrice ad retiarium, lotura post partum baptismo secundo. Et cum deducti essent in portam et cogerentur habitum induere, uiri quidem sacerdotum Saturni, feminae uero sacratarum Cereri, generosa illa in finem usque constantia repugnauit. Dicebat enim: Ideo ad hoc sponte peruenimus, ne libertas nostra obduceretur; ideo animam nostram addiximus, ne tale aliquid faceremus; hoc uobiscum pacti sumus. Agnouit iniustitia iustitiam: concessit tribunus, quomodo erant, simpliciter inducerentur. Perpetua psallebat, caput iam Aegyptii calcans; Reuocatus et Saturninus et Saturus populo spectanti comminabantur. Dehinc ut sub conspectu Hilariani peruenerint, gestu et nutu coeperunt Hilariano dicere: Tu nos, inquiunt, te autem deus. Ad hoc populus exasperatus flagellis eos uexari per ordinem uenatorum postulauit; et utique illi gratulati sunt quod aliquid et de dominicis passionibus essent consecuti.
thought_title: Walking into the arena in plain clothes
orientation: The anonymous redactor narrates in third person as the prisoners leave prison for the public games on the day of execution.
pass_a_gloss: The day of their victory dawned, and they marched out from the prison into the amphitheatre, as if into heaven, cheerful and beautiful in face; if trembling at all, trembling from joy, not from fear. Perpetua followed with calm step, as a married lady of Christ, as one beloved by God, casting down the gaze of all men by the vigor of her eyes. Also Felicity, rejoicing that she had given birth safely so that she might fight against the wild beasts, from blood to blood, from midwife to fighter with a net, about to wash after childbirth with a second baptism. And when they had been led down into the gate and were being compelled to put on clothing, the men indeed that of the priests of Saturn, the women indeed that of the consecrated women of Ceres, that noble constancy resisted to the very end. For she kept saying: For this reason we came to this of our own will, lest our freedom be covered over; for this reason we pledged our life, lest we do any such thing; this we agreed with you. Injustice recognized justice: the tribune conceded that just as they were, they be led in simply. Perpetua was singing a psalm, already trampling the head of the Egyptian; Revocatus and Saturninus and Saturus were threatening the watching people. Then when they came under the gaze of Hilarianus, by gesture and nod they began to say to Hilarianus: You judge us, they say, but God will judge you. At this the people, enraged, demanded that they be harassed with whips through the line of the hunters; and indeed they rejoiced that they had also obtained something from the sufferings of the Lord.

pass_b_english: The day of their victory dawned, and they walked out of the prison into the arena as if into heaven, cheerful and radiant in appearance. If they trembled at all, it was with joy and not with fear. Perpetua followed with a calm step, as a matron of Christ and as God's beloved, and the strength in her eyes made every onlooker look away. Felicity rejoiced that she had given birth safely and could now fight against the wild beasts, going from blood to blood, from the midwife to the net-fighter, to wash herself after her labor in a second baptism.

When they were brought to the gate and ordered to put on ritual dress, the men into the robes of the priests of Saturn and the women into the robes of the consecrated women of Ceres, that noble resolve resisted to the very end. Perpetua spoke for them: "We came to this place freely so our freedom would not be veiled. We pledged our lives so we would do no such thing. That is the agreement we made with you." Injustice recognized justice, and the tribune allowed them to be brought in simply wearing what they wore.

Perpetua sang a psalm as she went, already trampling the head of the Egyptian underfoot, while Revocatus, Saturninus, and Saturus threatened the watching crowd. Then, when they came into the sight of Hilarianus, they began to speak to him with gestures and nods: "You condemn us," they said, "but God will condemn you." The crowd was enraged at this and demanded that they be beaten with whips as they passed down the line of hunters. They were glad of it, because they had come to share even something of the sufferings of the Lord.
